subject: Secure ingress architecture for private deployment — peering vs endpoints vs encrypted tunnel

Subject: Private deployment connectivity options

Hi Jonas,

Thanks for the demo last week — our security and infra teams asked me to follow up. We're standing up a private deployment of Redwood in our VPC and need guidance on the ingress model. High-level constraints: we need encrypted traffic, no public internet exposure, and minimal changes to our existing peering.

Can you outline the pros/cons of: VPC peering, private endpoint (PrivateLink-style) into Redwood-managed subnets, and site-to-site VPN into a dedicated on-prem gateway? We have some network inventory attached and a rough sketch of our layout (see network_sketch.png).

Also please include any operational tradeoffs (routing, asymmetric paths, support implications) we should surface to our NetOps team.

Thanks — happy to loop in Tom from NetOps if helpful.

Hi Sarah — thanks for the details and the attachments. That's helpful.

I've sketched three customer-friendly summaries below and can schedule a short technical call with our infra lead (Vivek) and your NetOps folks. Proposed time: Thu 2027-06-03 10:00 PT. Does that work?

Quick summaries (high level):
- VPC peering: Lowest latency, simple routing for same-cloud VPCs, but creates a full-mesh routing surface and requires overlapping CIDR avoidance plus potential cross-account IAM/network coordination. Good if you want flat L3 access and can accept route propagation configuration.
- Private endpoints (Redwood-hosted PrivateLink): Strongest isolation (no route propagation into our control plane), minimal trust of Redwood network, supports per-endpoint policies and simplifies egress rules on your side. Slightly higher operational work on our side to provision endpoints and maintain scaling behind the endpoint.
- Site-to-site VPN: Useful for on-prem or multi-cloud when peering isn't viable. Adds encryption over the public internet and centralizes a single gateway, but introduces latency variability and makes autoscaling and NAT traversal more complicated. Also requires lifecycle ops on VPN tunnel keys and monitoring.

I'll prepare a one-pager and a recommended checklist for your NetOps team before the call. For the call invite, please share Tom's email or a Calendly slot.

Cheers,
Jonas

Internal note — Sarah at Acme needs a recommendation and will involve NetOps. Key asks: encrypted traffic, avoid public exposure, minimal changes to their peering.

My preference leaning: PrivateLink-style endpoint if we can offer per-customer endpoints that terminate in dedicated subnets. It reduces routing complexity on their side and keeps our control plane reachable with minimal ACL changes. Peering is attractive for latency but increases our blast radius and makes inter-customer route isolation harder. VPN is acceptable only if latency variability is tolerable and they want on-prem integration.

Please add your practical ops notes and any gotchas so I can send a customer-ready summary. Marissa — can you draft a short SOW placeholder? Lauren — throwing to you for any discount/credit guidance for a pilot.

Folks — technical deep-dive notes for the thread. Pasting succinct pros/cons and a recommended implementation pattern for Acme's constraints.

Option A — VPC peering (cross-account peering)- Pros:
  - Lowest RTT and predictable bandwidth inside cloud fabric
  - No extra proxy layer; straightforward to access internal endpoints- Cons:
  - Requires both sides to accept route propagation and manage overlapping CIDRs
  - Difficult to apply per-customer egress/ingress policy from our side without additional firewall appliances
  - Blast radius: if a customer misconfigures routes, it can impact our infra unless VPC segmentation is strict

Option B — Private endpoint (PrivateLink / AWS ENI-backed)- Pros:
  - Strong network isolation; customer's route only goes to the endpoint IP(s) we publish
  - Easier to enforce ACLs and per-customer policies; supports scalable LB behind endpoint
  - Compatible with cross-region endpoints in some providers; works well with our dedicated subnets approach- Cons:
  - Slightly higher per-connection management overhead (we provision endpoint services and maintain ENIs)
  - Need hardened monitoring on the endpoint plane for DDoS/connection storms
  - Small additional latency due to endpoint proxying (typically single-digit ms)

Option C — Site-to-site VPN / IPSec into our gateway- Pros:
  - Works for on-prem and multi-cloud customers where peering isn't an option
  - Encrypted by default; can terminate at a controlled gateway- Cons:
  - Variable latency and potential throughput constraints depending on customer's ISP and encryption device
  - Key rotation and tunnel maintenance is operational overhead
  - NAT/transit & health checks complicate autoscaling and multi-AZ redundancy

Recommendation for Acme (given their ask: encrypted, no public exposure, minimal changes):
  - Primary: Offer a PrivateLink-style endpoint into a customer-specific subnet group we manage. This gives isolation, minimal routing changes, and straightforward firewall config for Acme.
  - Fallback: If Acme insists on flat L3 connectivity for ultra-low latency across many flows, propose peering with strict ACLs and a limited CIDR carve-out; pair with route filters and proactive monitoring.
  - VPN: Offer as a supported alternate for their on-prem sites; warn about variability and include an SLA carve-out.

Operational checklist (short):
  - Confirm CIDR ranges and plan for non-overlapping /24 carve-outs
  - Validate route tables and ensure no unwanted route propagation
  - Plan endpoint scaling: target concurrent connections & NAT/per-ENI limits
  - KMS/HSM plan for any key material if we handle VPN termination
  - Monitoring: flow logs, endpoint health metrics, and alerting thresholds
  - Run a dry-run failover test for canary traffic

I'll draft a one-pager with this and a simple network diagram we can share.

—Vivek
VP Engineering, Inference Runtime

Hi Sarah — following up with a short customer-facing summary and proposed next steps (attached: redwood_private_options-sow-draft.docx). Key points:

- Recommended path: Private endpoint (Redwood-managed endpoint) to meet your requirements for encryption and no public exposure while minimizing changes to your VPC routing.
- Alternative: Cross-account VPC peering for lowest-latency flows — requires CIDR carve-out and route filtering on both sides.
- VPN: Supported for on-prem gateways; we'll include throughput testing and a tunnel lifecycle plan if you choose this.
